title: Lie-Algebraic Acceleration of Neural Koopman Dynamics
claim: Associative composition of segment-wise propagators lets sequential dynamics be computed in parallel with logarithmic depth via an upsweep and downsweep scan.
layout: 3 regions left-to-right: torus manifold, scan tree with braces, observable column
description: The figure has three regions, read left to right. On the left is a teal 3D torus labeled H, with a Lie algebra patch 𝔥 and a red arrow path made of Ω_θ^(k) steps. Axes are drawn and G points up. Teal lines connect these segments to the middle panel, which is a rounded green box holding a prefix-scan tree. Four rows (U0–U3) carry blue nodes and arrows, going through an upsweep (I) with B^(0), B^(1), B^(2) nodes and then a downsweep (II) back to ℓ=0. Braces under the box label the two phases. The right side is an 'Observable Space' column of teal nodes joined by red arrows. Each node is annotated with the Koopman operator approximations P_i and the predicted observables φ(x̂(t_i)). Teal and green dominate, and red marks the flow.
caption: Conceptual Illustration of Parallel Scan on Lie Algebra. Each red arrow corresponds to Ω(k)
abstract: We present a Lie-algebraic approach to model Koopman dynamics that integrates algebraic structure with computational scalability. The proposed formulation constrains the neural generators to evolve within prescribed Lie subalgebras and constructs finite-time flows through a neural Magnus expansion construction, thereby maintaining consistency with the associated Lie-group composition over each time segment. To address the computational burden inherent in sequential propagation, we exploit the associativity of Lie-group compositions and construct segmentwise propagators via a prefix-scan algorithm, which reduces the depth of temporal composition from linear to logarithmic. Consequently, the framework enables accurate long-horizon prediction while improving computational efficiency, and provides a principled foundation for scalable Koopman operator learning for nonlinear systems.
